In most locations, power grids have limited available capacity to support data center campuses ranging from several hundred megawatts to the gigawatt scale (or, as NVIDIA refers to them, AI factories). To address these capacity constraints in the near term, there are significant conversations around data center load flexibility. A 2025 report by Duke University’s Nicholas Institute estimates that modest curtailment of only 0.25–1% of annual consumption during critical hours could enable the grid to absorb up to 100 GW of new load without the need for new generation or other major upgrades (Norris et al. 2025). To mitigate the shortage of grid power, certain data center campuses are colocating energy generation capabilities, with the possibility of selling excess generation back to the grid (Bloomberg 2025). Some hyperscalers are demonstrating their load flexibility capabilities through workload scheduling (Terrell 2025) or through virtual power plant contracts (Voltus 2025). A recent PJM stakeholder review called out the need for load flexibility, the use of backup power generation in data center campuses, and load curtailment as options for assisting the grid (PJM 2025). In summary, the rapid demand for data centers is already stressing the grid and poses questions about how to continue to operate the grid reliably. The interaction between grid-side events and data center power systems at various timescales needs to be better understood, as data centers are on track to be a significant load on the grid. This understanding would help inform interconnection studies, policies, and regulations to assist with grid reliability. There are already new regulations and interconnection policies; a notable one is SB6 in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) territory, which can cause data centers to be shut down during grid emergency periods. Data center load has significantly evolved from being central processing unit-heavy uncorrelated workloads to being graphics processing unit-dominated and coordinated workloads. These workloads can go from an idle power state (10–20% of rated power) to a peak power state (80– 100% of rated power) within 10–100 milliseconds, exposing an oscillatory point of interconnection (POI) demand signal to the grid. AI workload frequencies fall into the subsynchronous regime. These can excite resonant modes in transmission networks, potentially leading to subsynchronous resonance or interarea oscillations. Further, rapid, cyclical power swings can lead to voltage flicker that is visible on lighting systems and frequency modulations that impact grid frequency regulation, particularly in isolated or constrained regions. NERC incident review (NERC 2025) reports approximately 1,500 MW of data center loads disconnecting from the grid due to short-duration grid faults (solely due to data center protection schemes) causing overvoltages (to 1.07 per unit [p.u.]) and overfrequencies (60.047 Hz), thus exposing risks of wide-area outages. With significant expansion on the demand and supply side, including behind-the-meter generation or energy storage capabilities to come, along with dynamic workloads, it is important to view this challenge from the lens of grid reliability.
